blocks.text: Ollama is a serving tool built around running large language models locally on consumer hardware, laptops and desktops, rather than data center GPUs, a distinctly different deployment target from the high-throughput production serving vLLM, covered in the previous topic, is built for.

This topic covers how Ollama uses GGUF format, covered in the earlier Model Export topic, its Modelfile system for configuring model behavior, and why it fits local development and personal use cases better than large-scale production traffic.
1. What Ollama Provides

blocks.alt: A GGUF model runs through Ollama, producing a local inference API

blocks.text: Ollama packages the GGUF format, covered in the earlier Model Export topic as optimized for efficient CPU and consumer hardware inference, into a simple command line tool and local API, making it straightforward to run a language model directly on a personal machine without data center infrastructure.
2. Data Center Serving vs Local Consumer Serving

blocks.alt: Data center GPU serving with vLLM or TensorRT-LLM is compared against local consumer serving with Ollama

blocks.text: Where vLLM and TensorRT-LLM, both covered in this module, target high-throughput serving on data center GPU hardware, Ollama specifically targets running models locally on whatever hardware a developer or individual user already has, a laptop CPU, a consumer GPU, or Apple Silicon, a fundamentally different deployment scenario.
3. Running a Model With Ollama

blocks.alt: ollama pull downloads a model, ollama run starts it running locally

blocks.text: Getting a model running with Ollama is typically a two-command process, pulling the model down and then running it, dramatically simpler than setting up the training-time libraries and serving infrastructure covered elsewhere in this module, a major reason for Ollama popularity among individual developers.

code.content:
ollama pull llama3
ollama run llama3 "Explain what a hash map is"

blocks.text: 4. Configuring Behavior With a Modelfile

blocks.alt: A Modelfile references a base model and sets system prompt and parameters

blocks.text: Ollama Modelfile lets a user define a custom model configuration, a base model reference, a default system prompt, generation parameters, all in a simple declarative file, conceptually similar to the YAML configuration approach covered in the earlier Axolotl topic, but focused on inference-time configuration rather than training.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Modelfile Directive","Purpose"],"rows":[["FROM","Specifies the base model to build on"],["SYSTEM","Sets a default system prompt"],["PARAMETER","Configures generation settings like temperature"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Hardware Flexibility

blocks.alt: Ollama runs across CPU inference, consumer GPU inference, and Apple Silicon inference

blocks.text: Ollama runs across a wide range of consumer hardware, plain CPU, consumer-grade GPUs, and Apple Silicon chips, automatically taking advantage of available acceleration where present, this hardware flexibility is a core part of what makes it approachable for individual developers without specialized infrastructure.

blocks.title: This hardware range is the whole point of Ollama
blocks.content: Unlike vLLM or TensorRT-LLM, both covered in this module and optimized for data center GPUs, Ollama design center is making inference genuinely practical on whatever machine a developer already owns.

blocks.text: 6. Deploying a Fine-Tuned Model Through Ollama

blocks.alt: A fine-tuned model exported to GGUF loads into Ollama

blocks.text: A model fine-tuned using the techniques covered throughout this course can be exported to GGUF format, covered in the earlier Model Export topic, and loaded into Ollama through a Modelfile, letting a custom fine-tuned model run locally with the same simple interface as any publicly available model.
7. Local Testing vs Production Scale Serving

blocks.alt: Developer local testing is distinct from production scale serving

blocks.text: Ollama is well suited to local development, testing, and personal use, but it is not designed to handle the high concurrent request volume a production deployment needs, for production scale serving, the throughput-optimized frameworks like vLLM or TensorRT-LLM, both covered in this module, are the appropriate choice instead.
8. Ollama in a Development Workflow

A common pattern is using Ollama locally during development and testing of an application that will eventually call a production-serving framework, letting developers iterate quickly without needing constant access to production infrastructure or cloud GPU costs during early development.
9. When Ollama Is the Right Choice

Ollama fits individual developers experimenting with models, local application development and testing, and genuinely local, privacy-sensitive use cases where running inference without sending data to any external server matters, it is not the right choice for serving significant production traffic.
Worked Example

A developer building an application that will eventually call a production vLLM deployment, covered in the previous topic, wants to iterate on their application logic locally without needing constant cloud GPU access. They export their fine-tuned model to GGUF format and load it into Ollama on their laptop.

This lets them develop and test their application prompts and logic entirely locally, switching to the actual production vLLM endpoint only once their application logic is stable, saving cloud costs and iteration time during the development phase.
Common Mistakes

items: Attempting to serve significant production traffic directly through Ollama instead of a throughput-optimized framework
Not exporting a fine-tuned model to GGUF format before attempting to load it into Ollama
Assuming Ollama and vLLM solve the same problem, when they target fundamentally different deployment scales and hardware
Overlooking Modelfile system prompt and parameter configuration, missing an easy way to customize local model behavior

blocks.text: Practice

For an application you are developing or could imagine developing, sketch a simple Ollama Modelfile setting a custom system prompt for your use case, and identify at what point in your development process you would switch from local Ollama testing to a production serving framework like vLLM.
Key Takeaway

Ollama runs language models locally on consumer hardware using the GGUF format covered in the earlier Model Export topic, with a simple command line interface and Modelfile configuration system, making it well suited to local development, testing, and personal use, but not a substitute for the production-scale, throughput-optimized serving frameworks like vLLM covered elsewhere in this module.
